Ken Mitchell is ready to lead. Ben Cline is still following Trump.

| | | | | [|

Ken Mitchell has spent his life in service — to his country, his community, and his family. A veteran with 24 years in the U.S. Army, a small business owner, and an infrastructure expert, Ken has the leadership and real-world experience we need in Congress.Ken has served in nonpartisan roles across federal agencies, contributed to major infrastructure and broadband projects in Virginia, and worked across the public and private sectors to deliver results. Whether leading telecommunications initiatives or restoring historic buildings, Ken knows how to solve problems — and he knows rural communities because he’s lived and worked in them.
---
|
---
| Meanwhile, our current representative, Ben Cline, continues to serve Trump’s extremist agenda — not the people of Virginia’s 6th District.**Here’s what you need to know:**
* Cline voted to overturn the results of the 2020 election — even after a violent insurrection.
* He co-sponsored legislation to withdraw the U.S. from the World Health Organization, jeopardizing our global health leadership.
* He’s stood by Trump’s chaos and remained silent on efforts to pardon January 6 rioters and other deeply anti-democratic actions.
* He’s ignored the urgent needs of this district — from rising costs to crumbling infrastructure to the lack of broadband access in rural communities.

Ben Cline’s priorities are clear: protect Trump, cut government services, and put big corporations first.He hasn’t delivered for working families. He’s delivered for party bosses and political donors.

As Pride Month comes to a close, I’ve been reflecting on the incredible progress we’ve made as well as the generations of LGBTQ+ leaders who fought to make it possible. Ten years ago today, marriage equality became the law of the land with the _Obergefell v. Hodges_ decision. It was a moment of joy, relief, and justice that only happened because generations of LGBTQ+ leaders and allies refused to give up the fight. We’ve made a lot of progress, but we can’t take anything for granted. We are living in a time where Republicans want to roll back our civil rights and challenge the legality of marriage equality. My opponent, David Schweikert, voted against marriage equality in 2022 and has a long anti-LGBTQ+ record. Our country is better when people can live authentically, free from hate and free from discrimination, and I will continue to fight for this version of our country. **[_When I’m in Congress, I will be a leader who protects and celebrates the diversity of all of our neighbors because that’s what makes our country strong. "**Justices side with Texas death row inmate seeking DNA testing to show he shouldn 't be executed,**" AP's **Mark Sherman** - "The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled for a [Texas death row inmate](https://substack.com/redirect/41656b4d-a482-4803-a03a-01b02d0e94af?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) who is seeking DNA testing to show he should be ineligible for execution.

The 6-3 decision in favor of **Ruben Gutierrez** gives him a potential path to have evidence tested that his lawyers say would help prove he was not responsible for the fatal stabbing of an 85-year-old woman during a home robbery decades ago.

His lawyers have said there was no physical or forensic evidence connecting him to the killing and that he was not a major participant in the crime. Two others also were charged in the case.

Gutierrez's lawyers argued that his case was similar to that of **Rodney Reed** , another longtime death row inmate in Texas who also won a round at the Supreme Court in his fight for DNA testing that he says would show he is innocent of murder.

In July, the high court granted Gutierrez a [stay](https://substack.com/redirect/8ead8e90-42a0-4040-a8d9-741dcf9fcccd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of execution 20 minutes before he was to receive a lethal injection.

[Gutierrez](https://substack.com/redirect/06214413-b15d-4c12-88ac-2e49a0018d45?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) was sentenced to death for the 1998 killing of **Escolastica Harrison** at her home in Brownsville in Texas' southern tip. Prosecutors said the killing of the mobile home park manager and retired teacher was part of an attempt to steal more than $600,000 that she had hidden in her home because of her mistrust of banks.

Gutierrez had several previous execution dates in recent years that were delayed, including [over issues](https://substack.com/redirect/1a522e9c-cc22-4f69-bb8a-92f8ee014051?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) related to [having a spiritual adviser in the death chamber](https://substack.com/redirect/47c34594-1492-44e6-82ea-8b48a5f482a8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). In June 2020, Gutierrez was [about an hour](https://substack.com/redirect/5c69b547-b460-47f9-9057-2a0ed52e0ed3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) from execution when he received a stay from the Supreme Court." "**How Bill Moyers Went from Marshall, Texas, to Being LBJ 's 'Young Man in Charge of Everything',**" Texas Monthly's **Joe Holley** - "On a sunny November afternoon in 1963, a slender, bespectacled young man hurried up the stairs of Air Force One at Love Field, in Dallas, and handed a scribbled note to a harried Secret Service agent who had failed to recognize him. "I'm here if you need me," the note read. Minutes later, the door to the front section of the plane opened, and the young man joined Vice President **Lyndon Johnson** minutes before he was sworn in as the nation's thirty-sixth president.

Johnson already knew then what Washington and the world would soon come to know. Young **Bill Moyers** , the pride of Marshall, Texas, was the indispensable man.

Moyers, who died on June 26 at 91, was like a son to the man who had two daughters but no sons of his own. A journalist, an ordained Baptist minister, and a remarkably adept practitioner of the political arts, he was an integral part of LBJ's ambitious effort to apply the power and resources of the federal government to the nation's knottiest challenges.

Arriving in Washington as a 25-year-old in 1959, he appeared to be the dark-suited, buttoned-down stereotype of the fifties organization man. The clean-cut young man knew how to get things done, things like the Peace Corps, which he helped design for President **John F. Kennedy** and for which he served as the first deputy director, under **Sargent Shriver**.

Working for LBJ in the White House, Moyers was involved in drafting the 1964, '65 and '66 civil rights bills (making him "persona no grata in my hometown," he told a reporter in 1984). As a domestic policy aide, he marshaled the multiple task forces that constructed LBJ's landmark Great Society programs, the preeminent accomplishments of Johnson's star-crossed presidency. He was involved in early discussions that led to the passage of the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, the legislation that established NPR and PBS. He made the cover of _Time_ magazine in October 1965 with a story headlined "L.B.J.'s Young Man in Charge of Everything."

LBJ's young man in charge also helped create one of the most memorable--some would say one of the most notorious--campaign ads in political history, the so-called "daisy" ad implying in the midst of the 1964 presidential race that a President **Barry Goldwater** was likely to blow up the world.

Moyers left the White House in 1966 and was a journalist for much longer than he was a presidential assistant. Over all those years, though, the ordained minister remained an evangelist of sorts for progressive causes and for the notion that a government of, by, and for the people should be harnessed to solve the people's problems. With the urgency of his beliefs leavened by a calm and sonorous East Texas twang and an earnest face, he became the voice of liberal causes--the conscience, so to speak, of broadcast news. His faith in his fellow man wavered at times, particularly during the troubled Trump era, but never completely evaporated." Hou Chron ($) "Justices side with Texas death row inmate seeking DNA testing to show he shouldn 't be executed," AP's Mark Sherman - "The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled for a who is seeking DNA testing to show he should be ineligible for execution. The 6-3 decision in favor of Ruben Gutierrez gives him a potential path to have evidence tested that his lawyers say would help prove he was not responsible for the fatal stabbing of an 85-year-old woman during a home robbery decades ago. His lawyers have said there was no physical or forensic evidence connecting him to the killing and that he was not a major participant in the crime. Two others also were charged in the case. Gutierrez's lawyers argued that his case was similar to that of Rodney Reed , another longtime death row inmate in Texas who also won a round at the Supreme Court in his fight for DNA testing that he says would show he is innocent of murder. In July, the high court granted Gutierrez a of execution 20 minutes before he was to receive a lethal injection. was sentenced to death for the 1998 killing of Escolastica Harrison at her home in Brownsville in Texas' southern tip. Prosecutors said the killing of the mobile home park manager and retired teacher was part of an attempt to steal more than $600,000 that she had hidden in her home because of her mistrust of banks. Gutierrez had several previous execution dates in recent years that were delayed, including related to . In June 2020, Gutierrez was from execution when he received a stay from the Supreme Court." "How Bill Moyers Went from Marshall, Texas, to Being LBJ 's 'Young Man in Charge of Everything'," Texas Monthly's Joe Holley - "On a sunny November afternoon in 1963, a slender, bespectacled young man hurried up the stairs of Air Force One at Love Field, in Dallas, and handed a scribbled note to a harried Secret Service agent who had failed to recognize him. "I'm here if you need me," the note read. Minutes later, the door to the front section of the plane opened, and the young man joined Vice President Lyndon Johnson minutes before he was sworn in as the nation's thirty-sixth president. Johnson already knew then what Washington and the world would soon come to know. Young Bill Moyers , the pride of Marshall, Texas, was the indispensable man. Moyers, who died on June 26 at 91, was like a son to the man who had two daughters but no sons of his own. A journalist, an ordained Baptist minister, and a remarkably adept practitioner of the political arts, he was an integral part of LBJ's ambitious effort to apply the power and resources of the federal government to the nation's knottiest challenges. Arriving in Washington as a 25-year-old in 1959, he appeared to be the dark-suited, buttoned-down stereotype of the fifties organization man. The clean-cut young man knew how to get things done, things like the Peace Corps, which he helped design for President John F. Kennedy and for which he served as the first deputy director, under Sargent Shriver. Working for LBJ in the White House, Moyers was involved in drafting the 1964, '65 and '66 civil rights bills (making him "persona no grata in my hometown," he told a reporter in 1984). As a domestic policy aide, he marshaled the multiple task forces that constructed LBJ's landmark Great Society programs, the preeminent accomplishments of Johnson's star-crossed presidency. He was involved in early discussions that led to the passage of the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, the legislation that established NPR and PBS. He made the cover of Time magazine in October 1965 with a story headlined "L.B.J.'s Young Man in Charge of Everything." LBJ's young man in charge also helped create one of the most memorable--some would say one of the most notorious--campaign ads in political history, the so-called "daisy" ad implying in the midst of the 1964 presidential race that a President Barry Goldwater was likely to blow up the world. Moyers left the White House in 1966 and was a journalist for much longer than he was a presidential assistant. Over all those years, though, the ordained minister remained an evangelist of sorts for progressive causes and for the notion that a government of, by, and for the people should be harnessed to solve the people's problems. With the urgency of his beliefs leavened by a calm and sonorous East Texas twang and an earnest face, he became the voice of liberal causes--the conscience, so to speak, of broadcast news. His faith in his fellow man wavered at times, particularly during the troubled Trump era, but never completely evaporated." Hey friend, it’s Mark Kelly. My friend Chris Pappas is running for Senate in New Hampshire and needs our help. It's official, team.
**Scott Brown just announced he’s running to flip New Hampshire’s Senate seat red.**
If that name sounds familiar, it’s because he’s run for Senate — and lost — before. In Massachusetts. Then he ran here, hoping Granite Staters wouldn’t notice. But we did.
Now he’s back, with support from the national Republican machine, trying to buy his way into the Senate again. It’s up to our grassroots team to stop him.
[**Please, split a $3 contribution now between my campaign and Mark Kelly and join the fight to beat Scott Brown.**](https://act.markkelly.com/go/1389?c0=partner_ms_cp_em_kelly.9qM-X9&refcode=em250626-1-90&t=2&akid=6102%2E6688874%2E6c2erD)
**This is a serious threat.** The GOP sees New Hampshire as one of their best chances to expand their Senate majority — and they’re counting on Scott Brown to help them do it.
_But this seat doesn’t belong to Scott Brown._ It belongs to the people of New Hampshire.
I was born and raised here. I’ve run a family business, represented our communities in Concord and in Congress, and delivered for the people who call this state home — from lowering prescription drug costs to defending reproductive freedom and our democracy.
Scott Brown’s record is clear:
* ❌ He supports Trump’s MAGA agenda.
* ❌ He voted to defund Planned Parenthood.
* ❌ He opposed marriage equality and the Affordable Care Act.

That’s not who we are. And that’s not who should represent us.
This race is now one of the most competitive in the country — and the GOP is ready to pour millions into this race to try to win it and expand the Republican Senate majority.
**But we’ve beaten Scott Brown before. And with your help, we’ll do it again.**

"**Justices side with Texas death row inmate seeking DNA testing to show he shouldn 't be executed,**" AP's **Mark Sherman** - "The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled for a [Texas death row inmate](https://substack.com/redirect/d2b78885-9a2b-4c84-95ca-cc38377ea250?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) who is seeking DNA testing to show he should be ineligible for execution.

The 6-3 decision in favor of **Ruben Gutierrez** gives him a potential path to have evidence tested that his lawyers say would help prove he was not responsible for the fatal stabbing of an 85-year-old woman during a home robbery decades ago.

His lawyers have said there was no physical or forensic evidence connecting him to the killing and that he was not a major participant in the crime. Two others also were charged in the case.

Gutierrez's lawyers argued that his case was similar to that of **Rodney Reed** , another longtime death row inmate in Texas who also won a round at the Supreme Court in his fight for DNA testing that he says would show he is innocent of murder.

In July, the high court granted Gutierrez a [stay](https://substack.com/redirect/0b6c391c-139b-4637-a789-252a36881496?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of execution 20 minutes before he was to receive a lethal injection.

[Gutierrez](https://substack.com/redirect/9b31435b-f92a-44fa-ba2b-87318a8ee541?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) was sentenced to death for the 1998 killing of **Escolastica Harrison** at her home in Brownsville in Texas' southern tip. Prosecutors said the killing of the mobile home park manager and retired teacher was part of an attempt to steal more than $600,000 that she had hidden in her home because of her mistrust of banks.

Gutierrez had several previous execution dates in recent years that were delayed, including [over issues](https://substack.com/redirect/67bb98c5-1594-4602-a483-6087caa9bf25?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) related to [having a spiritual adviser in the death chamber](https://substack.com/redirect/70536a76-2f5c-435b-9c6d-6a1c1649a52c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). In June 2020, Gutierrez was [about an hour](https://substack.com/redirect/7bf77868-b56a-4f66-8b72-3cab3a729a12?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) from execution when he received a stay from the Supreme Court." "**How Bill Moyers Went from Marshall, Texas, to Being LBJ 's 'Young Man in Charge of Everything',**" Texas Monthly's **Joe Holley** - "On a sunny November afternoon in 1963, a slender, bespectacled young man hurried up the stairs of Air Force One at Love Field, in Dallas, and handed a scribbled note to a harried Secret Service agent who had failed to recognize him. "I'm here if you need me," the note read. Minutes later, the door to the front section of the plane opened, and the young man joined Vice President **Lyndon Johnson** minutes before he was sworn in as the nation's thirty-sixth president.

Johnson already knew then what Washington and the world would soon come to know. Young **Bill Moyers** , the pride of Marshall, Texas, was the indispensable man.

Moyers, who died on June 26 at 91, was like a son to the man who had two daughters but no sons of his own. A journalist, an ordained Baptist minister, and a remarkably adept practitioner of the political arts, he was an integral part of LBJ's ambitious effort to apply the power and resources of the federal government to the nation's knottiest challenges.

Arriving in Washington as a 25-year-old in 1959, he appeared to be the dark-suited, buttoned-down stereotype of the fifties organization man. The clean-cut young man knew how to get things done, things like the Peace Corps, which he helped design for President **John F. Kennedy** and for which he served as the first deputy director, under **Sargent Shriver**.

Working for LBJ in the White House, Moyers was involved in drafting the 1964, '65 and '66 civil rights bills (making him "persona no grata in my hometown," he told a reporter in 1984). As a domestic policy aide, he marshaled the multiple task forces that constructed LBJ's landmark Great Society programs, the preeminent accomplishments of Johnson's star-crossed presidency. He was involved in early discussions that led to the passage of the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, the legislation that established NPR and PBS. He made the cover of _Time_ magazine in October 1965 with a story headlined "L.B.J.'s Young Man in Charge of Everything."

LBJ's young man in charge also helped create one of the most memorable--some would say one of the most notorious--campaign ads in political history, the so-called "daisy" ad implying in the midst of the 1964 presidential race that a President **Barry Goldwater** was likely to blow up the world.

Moyers left the White House in 1966 and was a journalist for much longer than he was a presidential assistant. Over all those years, though, the ordained minister remained an evangelist of sorts for progressive causes and for the notion that a government of, by, and for the people should be harnessed to solve the people's problems. With the urgency of his beliefs leavened by a calm and sonorous East Texas twang and an earnest face, he became the voice of liberal causes--the conscience, so to speak, of broadcast news. His faith in his fellow man wavered at times, particularly during the troubled Trump era, but never completely evaporated." TOP NEWS "CenterPoint outages affecting over 10K in Houston during heavy rain, " Houston Chronicle's Alexia Partouche - "Thursday's downpours interrupted electrical service to thousands of Houston-area residents. CenterPoint is reporting more than 400 outages in the Houston area because of on Thursday, impacting upwards of 10,000 customers, according to its . The most outages have been reported in Greenspoint, according to the ." Hou Chron ($) "Justices side with Texas death row inmate seeking DNA testing to show he shouldn 't be executed," AP's Mark Sherman - "The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled for a who is seeking DNA testing to show he should be ineligible for execution. The 6-3 decision in favor of Ruben Gutierrez gives him a potential path to have evidence tested that his lawyers say would help prove he was not responsible for the fatal stabbing of an 85-year-old woman during a home robbery decades ago. His lawyers have said there was no physical or forensic evidence connecting him to the killing and that he was not a major participant in the crime. Two others also were charged in the case. Gutierrez's lawyers argued that his case was similar to that of Rodney Reed , another longtime death row inmate in Texas who also won a round at the Supreme Court in his fight for DNA testing that he says would show he is innocent of murder. In July, the high court granted Gutierrez a of execution 20 minutes before he was to receive a lethal injection. was sentenced to death for the 1998 killing of Escolastica Harrison at her home in Brownsville in Texas' southern tip. Prosecutors said the killing of the mobile home park manager and retired teacher was part of an attempt to steal more than $600,000 that she had hidden in her home because of her mistrust of banks. Gutierrez had several previous execution dates in recent years that were delayed, including related to . In June 2020, Gutierrez was from execution when he received a stay from the Supreme Court." "How Bill Moyers Went from Marshall, Texas, to Being LBJ 's 'Young Man in Charge of Everything'," Texas Monthly's Joe Holley - "On a sunny November afternoon in 1963, a slender, bespectacled young man hurried up the stairs of Air Force One at Love Field, in Dallas, and handed a scribbled note to a harried Secret Service agent who had failed to recognize him. "I'm here if you need me," the note read. Minutes later, the door to the front section of the plane opened, and the young man joined Vice President Lyndon Johnson minutes before he was sworn in as the nation's thirty-sixth president. Johnson already knew then what Washington and the world would soon come to know. Young Bill Moyers , the pride of Marshall, Texas, was the indispensable man. Moyers, who died on June 26 at 91, was like a son to the man who had two daughters but no sons of his own. A journalist, an ordained Baptist minister, and a remarkably adept practitioner of the political arts, he was an integral part of LBJ's ambitious effort to apply the power and resources of the federal government to the nation's knottiest challenges. Arriving in Washington as a 25-year-old in 1959, he appeared to be the dark-suited, buttoned-down stereotype of the fifties organization man. The clean-cut young man knew how to get things done, things like the Peace Corps, which he helped design for President John F. Kennedy and for which he served as the first deputy director, under Sargent Shriver. Working for LBJ in the White House, Moyers was involved in drafting the 1964, '65 and '66 civil rights bills (making him "persona no grata in my hometown," he told a reporter in 1984). As a domestic policy aide, he marshaled the multiple task forces that constructed LBJ's landmark Great Society programs, the preeminent accomplishments of Johnson's star-crossed presidency. He was involved in early discussions that led to the passage of the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, the legislation that established NPR and PBS. He made the cover of Time magazine in October 1965 with a story headlined "L.B.J.'s Young Man in Charge of Everything." LBJ's young man in charge also helped create one of the most memorable--some would say one of the most notorious--campaign ads in political history, the so-called "daisy" ad implying in the midst of the 1964 presidential race that a President Barry Goldwater was likely to blow up the world. Moyers left the White House in 1966 and was a journalist for much longer than he was a presidential assistant. Over all those years, though, the ordained minister remained an evangelist of sorts for progressive causes and for the notion that a government of, by, and for the people should be harnessed to solve the people's problems. With the urgency of his beliefs leavened by a calm and sonorous East Texas twang and an earnest face, he became the voice of liberal causes--the conscience, so to speak, of broadcast news. His faith in his fellow man wavered at times, particularly during the troubled Trump era, but never completely evaporated." “**How Bill Moyers Went from Marshall, Texas, to Being LBJ’s 'Young Man in Charge of Everything',**” Texas Monthly's **Joe Holley** – “On a sunny November afternoon in 1963, a slender, bespectacled young man hurried up the stairs of Air Force One at Love Field, in Dallas, and handed a scribbled note to a harried Secret Service agent who had failed to recognize him. “I’m here if you need me,” the note read. Minutes later, the door to the front section of the plane opened, and the young man joined Vice President **Lyndon Johnson** minutes before he was sworn in as the nation’s thirty-sixth president.

Johnson already knew then what Washington and the world would soon come to know. Young **Bill Moyers** , the pride of Marshall, Texas, was the indispensable man.

Moyers, who died on June 26 at 91, was like a son to the man who had two daughters but no sons of his own. A journalist, an ordained Baptist minister, and a remarkably adept practitioner of the political arts, he was an integral part of LBJ’s ambitious effort to apply the power and resources of the federal government to the nation’s knottiest challenges.

Arriving in Washington as a 25-year-old in 1959, he appeared to be the dark-suited, buttoned-down stereotype of the fifties organization man. The clean-cut young man knew how to get things done, things like the Peace Corps, which he helped design for President **John F. Kennedy** and for which he served as the first deputy director, under **Sargent Shriver**.

Working for LBJ in the White House, Moyers was involved in drafting the 1964, ’65 and ’66 civil rights bills (making him “persona no grata in my hometown,” he told a reporter in 1984). As a domestic policy aide, he marshaled the multiple task forces that constructed LBJ’s landmark Great Society programs, the preeminent accomplishments of Johnson’s star-crossed presidency. He was involved in early discussions that led to the passage of the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, the legislation that established NPR and PBS. He made the cover of _Time_ magazine in October 1965 with a story headlined “L.B.J.’s Young Man in Charge of Everything.”

LBJ’s young man in charge also helped create one of the most memorable—some would say one of the most notorious—campaign ads in political history, the so-called “daisy” ad implying in the midst of the 1964 presidential race that a President **Barry Goldwater** was likely to blow up the world.

Moyers left the White House in 1966 and was a journalist for much longer than he was a presidential assistant. Over all those years, though, the ordained minister remained an evangelist of sorts for progressive causes and for the notion that a government of, by, and for the people should be harnessed to solve the people’s problems. With the urgency of his beliefs leavened by a calm and sonorous East Texas twang and an earnest face, he became the voice of liberal causes—the conscience, so to speak, of broadcast news. His faith in his fellow man wavered at times, particularly during the troubled Trump era, but never completely evaporated." ($) » » “Justices side with Texas death row inmate seeking DNA testing to show he shouldn’t be executed, ” AP's Mark Sherman – “The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled for a who is seeking DNA testing to show he should be ineligible for execution. The 6-3 decision in favor of Ruben Gutierrez gives him a potential path to have evidence tested that his lawyers say would help prove he was not responsible for the fatal stabbing of an 85-year-old woman during a home robbery decades ago. His lawyers have said there was no physical or forensic evidence connecting him to the killing and that he was not a major participant in the crime. Two others also were charged in the case. Gutierrez’s lawyers argued that his case was similar to that of Rodney Reed , another longtime death row inmate in Texas who also won a round at the Supreme Court in his fight for DNA testing that he says would show he is innocent of murder. In July, the high court granted Gutierrez a of execution 20 minutes before he was to receive a lethal injection. was sentenced to death for the 1998 killing of Escolastica Harrison at her home in Brownsville in Texas’ southern tip. Prosecutors said the killing of the mobile home park manager and retired teacher was part of an attempt to steal more than $600,000 that she had hidden in her home because of her mistrust of banks. Gutierrez had several previous execution dates in recent years that were delayed, including related to . In June 2020, Gutierrez was from execution when he received a stay from the Supreme Court." “How Bill Moyers Went from Marshall, Texas, to Being LBJ’s 'Young Man in Charge of Everything',” Texas Monthly's Joe Holley – “On a sunny November afternoon in 1963, a slender, bespectacled young man hurried up the stairs of Air Force One at Love Field, in Dallas, and handed a scribbled note to a harried Secret Service agent who had failed to recognize him. “I’m here if you need me,” the note read. Minutes later, the door to the front section of the plane opened, and the young man joined Vice President Lyndon Johnson minutes before he was sworn in as the nation’s thirty-sixth president. Johnson already knew then what Washington and the world would soon come to know. Young Bill Moyers , the pride of Marshall, Texas, was the indispensable man. Moyers, who died on June 26 at 91, was like a son to the man who had two daughters but no sons of his own. A journalist, an ordained Baptist minister, and a remarkably adept practitioner of the political arts, he was an integral part of LBJ’s ambitious effort to apply the power and resources of the federal government to the nation’s knottiest challenges. Arriving in Washington as a 25-year-old in 1959, he appeared to be the dark-suited, buttoned-down stereotype of the fifties organization man. The clean-cut young man knew how to get things done, things like the Peace Corps, which he helped design for President John F. Kennedy and for which he served as the first deputy director, under Sargent Shriver. Working for LBJ in the White House, Moyers was involved in drafting the 1964, ’65 and ’66 civil rights bills (making him “persona no grata in my hometown,” he told a reporter in 1984). As a domestic policy aide, he marshaled the multiple task forces that constructed LBJ’s landmark Great Society programs, the preeminent accomplishments of Johnson’s star-crossed presidency. He was involved in early discussions that led to the passage of the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, the legislation that established NPR and PBS. He made the cover of Time magazine in October 1965 with a story headlined “L.B.J.’s Young Man in Charge of Everything.” LBJ’s young man in charge also helped create one of the most memorable—some would say one of the most notorious—campaign ads in political history, the so-called “daisy” ad implying in the midst of the 1964 presidential race that a President Barry Goldwater was likely to blow up the world. Moyers left the White House in 1966 and was a journalist for much longer than he was a presidential assistant. Over all those years, though, the ordained minister remained an evangelist of sorts for progressive causes and for the notion that a government of, by, and for the people should be harnessed to solve the people’s problems. With the urgency of his beliefs leavened by a calm and sonorous East Texas twang and an earnest face, he became the voice of liberal causes—the conscience, so to speak, of broadcast news. His faith in his fellow man wavered at times, particularly during the troubled Trump era, but never completely evaporated." | FREE SUBSCRIPTIONS HAVE ENDED : As of July 11, 2022, we have moved to a paywall for free subscribers.
